title: Decisions: booleans and if
summary: Ask yes/no questions with comparisons, and let the answer choose which code runs.
license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner
objective: Choose between actions with if, elif and else, using comparisons, and, or, not and truthiness.
analogy: An if statement is a fork in a path with signposts: Python reads the signs top to bottom and takes the first road whose sign is true.

misconceptions.belief: Every true branch of an if/elif chain runs.
misconceptions.correction: Only the first true branch runs; the rest are skipped.

misconceptions.belief: `if x == 1 or 2:` checks whether x is 1 or 2.
misconceptions.correction: It means `(x == 1) or 2`, which is always truthy; write `x == 1 or x == 2`.

misconceptions.belief: Only True and False can be used as conditions.
misconceptions.correction: Any value has a truth value: 0, "", [] and None are falsy, almost everything else is truthy.

rubric.evidence: values exactly on each limit go to the right branch
conditions are checked in an order where the first match is the right one
flags work for any truthy or falsy value, not just True and False

review.recall: In an if/elif/else chain, how many branches can run? What are four falsy values?

steps.title: Programs that decide
steps.body:
So far every line of your programs has run, top to bottom, every time. Real programs react: a shop charges
children less, a thermostat switches on only when it's cold, a login form refuses a wrong password.

Each of those is a **question with a yes-or-no answer**, followed by different actions depending on the
answer. This lesson gives you both halves: how Python asks the question, and how it picks what to do next.

steps.title: A comparison is a question
steps.body:
Writing `temp < 10` doesn't *do* anything to `temp`. It **asks** "is temp less than 10?" and Python
answers with one of exactly two values: `True` or `False`. These two values have their own type, `bool`
(short for *boolean*). They are not the text "True" and "False"; they're values, like `7` is a value.

An `if` statement is a fork in the road. Python evaluates the question once, and the answer decides which path
the program takes. The path that isn't taken is skipped entirely, as if those lines weren't there.

questions: What do you think `print(3 > 2)` shows? Is it text, a number, or something else?
If a condition is checked and is False, does Python ever come back to it later on its own?

steps.title: Watch Python choose a branch
steps.body:
Step through and watch which conditions are **checked**, and which lines are **skipped**. Only one branch
ever runs.

frames.note: The `def` stores the function. Nothing inside it runs yet.
To print, Python first needs the value of `describe(18)`, so it makes the call.
First question: is `18 < 10`? The answer is `False`, so the `return "cold"` line is skipped.
`elif` asks the next question only because the first answer was False: is `18 < 25`? `True`.
This branch runs and returns "mild". The `else` branch is never looked at.
The call is over and `print` shows the returned text.

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Comparisons** produce a `bool`: `==` equal, `!=` not equal, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`.
Note the doubled `==`. A single `=` *assigns* a name, so `if x = 5:` is a `SyntaxError`.

**Logical operators** combine bools: `a and b` is True only when both are; `a or b` is True when at
least one is; `not a` flips it.

```python
if condition:
    ...            # runs when condition is true
elif other_condition:
    ...            # checked only if everything above was false
else:
    ...            # runs when nothing above was true
```

1. The conditions are checked **in order**, and the **first** true one wins. Its block runs, and the whole
   statement ends. Later conditions are not checked, even if they would also be true.
2. `elif` and `else` are optional. There may be any number of `elif`s, and `else` must come last.
3. A block is the indented lines under its header, exactly as in a `def`.
4. **Truthiness:** any value can be a condition. `0`, `0.0`, `""` (empty text) and `None` count as
   false; other numbers and non-empty text count as true. Prefer an explicit comparison such as
   `if count == 0:` when it states your intent more clearly.

steps.title: Run it: ticket prices
steps.body:
Under 5s go free; children and over-65s pay the reduced price. Predict all four lines, then **Run**.
Which branch handles age 70, and why doesn't it reach the `else`?

steps.title: Your turn: even or odd
steps.body:
Complete `parity(n)` so it **returns** the text `"even"` when `n` is even and `"odd"` otherwise.

The remainder operator `%` helps: `n % 2` is `0` exactly when `n` divides evenly by 2.
hints: Use an if/else: one branch returns "even", the other returns "odd".
The question to ask is whether `n % 2 == 0`.

tests.name: 0 is even
tests.code: assert parity(0) == 'even', f'parity(0) returned {parity(0)!r}; 0 divides by 2 with no remainder'

steps.title: Challenge: leap years
steps.body:
In the Gregorian calendar a year is a leap year if it divides by 4, **except** years that divide by 100,
which are leap years only if they also divide by 400. So 2024 is a leap year, 1900 is not, and 2000 is.

Write `is_leap(year)` that **returns** `True` or `False` (bools, not text). Order your checks carefully;
remember that the first true condition wins.
hints: The starter gets 1900 wrong. Which rule does it ignore?
Check the most specific rule first: divisible by 400, then by 100, then by 4.
Or in one expression: divisible by 4 and (not divisible by 100, or divisible by 400).

def is_leap(year):
    return year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)

tests.name: ordinary leap year
tests.code: assert is_leap(2024) is True, f'is_leap(2024) returned {is_leap(2024)!r}'

tests.name: ordinary year
tests.code: assert is_leap(2023) is False, f'is_leap(2023) returned {is_leap(2023)!r}'

tests.name: century, not leap
tests.code: assert is_leap(1900) is False, f'is_leap(1900) returned {is_leap(1900)!r}: centuries need to divide by 400'

tests.name: divisible by 400
tests.code: assert is_leap(2000) is True, f'is_leap(2000) returned {is_leap(2000)!r}'

tests.name: returns a bool
tests.code: assert type(is_leap(1996)) is bool, 'Return True or False, not text or a number'

steps.title: Transfer: cinema tickets
steps.body:
Write `ticket_price(age, student)`. Children under 3 go free (0). Ages 3 to 12 pay 6, and 65 or over pay 7. Everyone
else pays 10, except that a student (any truthy `student` value) aged 13 to 64 pays 8.
hints: Check the age bands from the youngest up: `if age < 3`, `elif age <= 12`, `elif age >= 65`.
In the last case, `return 8 if student else 10` uses the flag's truthiness.

tests.name: the age bands
tests.code: assert [ticket_price(a, False) for a in (0, 5, 30, 70)] == [0, 6, 10, 7], [ticket_price(a, False) for a in (0, 5, 30, 70)]

tests.name: ages exactly on the limits
tests.code: assert [ticket_price(a, False) for a in (2, 3, 12, 13, 64, 65)] == [0, 6, 6, 10, 10, 7], [ticket_price(a, False) for a in (2, 3, 12, 13, 64, 65)]

tests.name: students pay 8 only aged 13 to 64
tests.code: assert ticket_price(20, True) == 8 and ticket_price(10, True) == 6 and ticket_price(70, True) == 7, 'the student price is for ages 13 to 64'

tests.name: any truthy value counts as a student
tests.code:
assert ticket_price(20, 'yes') == 8 and ticket_price(20, 1) == 8
assert ticket_price(20, '') == 10 and ticket_price(20, 0) == 10 and ticket_price(20, None) == 10

tests.name: returns numbers
tests.code: assert all(isinstance(ticket_price(a, s), int) for a in (1, 40) for s in (True, False))

steps.title: Check your understanding
steps.body: Answer each one before running anything.

questions.explanation: Both `x > 10` and `x > 5` are true, but only the first true branch runs; then the statement ends.
Zero (including `0.0`) counts as false in a condition, so the `else` branch runs.

questions.prompt: What happens when Python reads `if score = 100:`?
choices: It sets score to 100, then runs the block
questions.explanation: `=` assigns and `==` compares. Python refuses an assignment where a condition belongs.

questions.prompt: What is the value of `not (3 > 2 and 2 > 5)`?
questions.explanation: `3 > 2` is True and `2 > 5` is False, so the `and` is False, and `not False` is True.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Ask questions with comparisons and combine them with `and`, `or` and `not`.
- Explain that `True` and `False` are values of type `bool`.
- Write `if` / `elif` / `else` chains and predict which single branch runs.
- Say which values count as false in a condition, and when an explicit comparison reads better.

Next: repeating code with loops, where a condition decides when to **stop**.
